Rusty blenny (Parablennius sanguinolentus) exhibits life-history traits typical of a small benthic teleost inhabiting shallow rocky substrates of the Mediterranean and adjacent Atlantic coasts. Field surveys along the Ligurian coast have documented that the total length at which individuals attain sexual maturity is approximately 9 centimetres [Lp = approximately 9 centimetres], a value that aligns with observations in related blenniid species such as Parablennius ruber. This length threshold corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence, after which reproductive activity becomes cyclical. The species is iteroparous, with spawning events concentrated during the warmer months. In a controlled laboratory setting maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was measured at approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%]. This figure was calculated from dissected gravid females and falls within the lower range reported for sympatric blenniids, suggesting that reproductive effort may be constrained by the energetic demands of territory defence and nest guarding.

Embryonic development in this species proceeds relatively rapidly under stable thermal regimes. Eggs deposited beneath stones in the intertidal zone are guarded by the male parent until the prolarvae emerge. At a constant water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 15.5 days [ab = approximately 15.5 days], a developmental duration that is typical for blenniid fishes breeding in temperate waters. The emerging yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous nutrition during the first few days post-hatching. The wet weight at birth of these newly hatched individuals is exceedingly low, estimated at 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams] based on the dimensions of the demersal egg, which measures roughly 1.1 millimetres in length and 0.6 millimetres in width. This minute initial mass imposes a tight energetic bottleneck during the transition to exogenous feeding, as the resorption of the yolk sac must be completed before the mouth becomes fully functional for prey capture.

As the larvae progress through the pelagic phase, they undergo a pronounced allometric shift during metamorphosis prior to settlement into a benthic habitat. Following settlement, immature juveniles begin a phase of rapid somatic growth that continues until they approach their asymptotic body dimensions. The ultimate total length recorded for adult Parablennius sanguinolentus based on extensive field sampling is 20 centimetres [Li = 20 centimetres], a size that is seldom exceeded even in long-established individuals. Corresponding to this length, the ultimate wet weight derived from the length-weight relationship fitted for this species reaches approximately 102 grams [Wwi = approximately 102 grams]. These maxima place the Rusty blenny among the larger members of its genus, although considerable variation exists across its geographic range, likely reflecting local differences in food availability and thermal regime.

Longevity under natural conditions is another key parameter that shapes the species' demography. Mark-recapture studies conducted over a decade in the northwestern Mediterranean have provided estimates of maximum lifespan. At a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], which is equivalent to about 3650 days under captive maintenance. This relatively extended lifespan for a fish of its size is consistent with a life-history strategy that emphasises repeated breeding over multiple seasons rather than a single, high-investment reproductive bout. Older individuals often exhibit slower growth rates but maintain reproductive output, suggesting that senescence in this species is gradual rather than catastrophic. The ability to survive across several annual cycles likely confers a demographic advantage in variable coastal environments where recruitment success fluctuates considerably.

Comparative physiological studies have examined how the Rusty blenny's metabolic and reproductive traits relate to those of congeneric species inhabiting similar thermal niches. At the same laboratory temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the age at birth or hatching duration of approximately 15.5 days [ab = approximately 15.5 days] closely mirrors values reported for Parablennius ruber, reinforcing the phylogenetic conservatism of early developmental rates within the genus. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The total length at puberty of 9 centimetres [Lp = 9 centimetres] and the ultimate total length of 20 centimetres [Li = 20 centimetres] together delineate a relatively broad reproductive window during which females can contribute multiple clutches annually, thereby buffering against poor recruitment years.
